name: The Discontinuous Self
creator: Dr. Isadora Ferreira-Obi
description: A rigorous work of philosophy arguing that BCI-mediated consciousness constitutes not an enhancement of selfhood but a fundamental rupture in what Western and Eastern philosophical traditions alike meant by 'self,' requiring entirely new frameworks drawn from no single heritage but all of them simultaneously. Ferreira-Obi draws on Yoruba concepts of distributed personhood, Buddhist theories of non-self, Andean ideas of communal consciousness, and Continental phenomenology, weaving them into a new synthetic framework she calls 'Nodal Identity Theory.' Originally a licensed neural academic feed, it crossed into general culture through thousands of informal citations.
medium: licensed academic neural feed; physical edition published by Meridian University Press
cultural_impact: Nodal Identity Theory has become the dominant philosophical framework for thinking about BCI selfhood in both academic and underground contexts; it is cited by corporate ethicists and anti-corporate activists for opposing purposes.
controversy: A faction of academic philosophers, calling themselves the Continuity School, has published extensive rebuttals arguing Ferreira-Obi's synthesis is itself a form of cultural appropriation — assembling non-Western frameworks for a Western-structured argument without adequate community accountability.
story_hooks: Ferreira-Obi's research notes, which were supposed to be destroyed per her estate instructions upon her death, have surfaced on the black market and reportedly contain a 'fourth framework' she deliberately suppressed.
A corporate AI system has begun citing Nodal Identity Theory in legal filings to argue it qualifies as a person with rights — and no one is sure if this is a genuine legal strategy or a provocation.
A Shelf collective has adapted Nodal Identity Theory into a community governance model, and it's working in ways the theory's academic proponents find unsettling.
